Priam is a French-bred apple carrying genetic immunity to apple scab, one of the most damaging and widespread apple diseases, particularly troublesome in humid climates where standard varieties require regular fungicide applications to produce clean fruit. The medium-sized, red-blushed fruit has crisp, juicy, well-balanced flesh suitable for both fresh eating and cooking, and while it may not match the absolute peak flavor of the finest dessert apples, its dramatically reduced spray requirements make it an attractive option for organic growers and home gardeners wanting to minimize chemical inputs. As with other scab-immune apples, some resistance can erode with new scab races over time, so continued monitoring is worthwhile even on a genetically resistant tree.

Shenandoah came out of the cooperative Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) disease-resistant apple breeding program, which focused on combining genetic resistance to scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew into apples that also deliver good eating quality, reducing the spray program needed to produce clean fruit in humid, disease-prone regions. The fruit is crisp and well flavored, with red-striped skin over a yellow background, suitable for fresh eating and general kitchen use. For home orchardists in the humid South and Mid-Atlantic dealing with heavy disease pressure, multi-resistant PRI-program apples like Shenandoah offer a meaningfully easier path to a clean home apple crop than many older, disease-susceptible heirloom varieties.

Nova Easygro was released by the Nova Scotia agricultural research program specifically for scab resistance and generally easy, low-input growing, living up to its name by requiring far less fungicide intervention than scab-susceptible standard varieties to produce clean, attractive fruit. The medium, red-striped apple has crisp, juicy flesh with a pleasant, mild sweet-tart flavor good for fresh eating and general cooking use. Its combination of disease resistance and straightforward care requirements has made it a practical recommendation for home orchardists in humid, scab-prone regions who want to grow apples with a minimal spray program, particularly those interested in organic or low-chemical fruit production.

St. Edmund's Pippin originated in Bury St Edmunds, England, in the 1870s, prized as one of the finest early russet dessert apples, with golden-yellow, rough-textured russeted skin covering crisp, aromatic, richly flavored flesh with a distinctive nutty sweetness characteristic of the best russet apples. It ripens earlier than most other russets, extending the season for gardeners who enjoy this distinctive style of apple beyond the typical late-fall russet harvest. The tree bears reliably and the fruit, while not a long keeper, offers exceptional eating quality fresh off the tree, making it a favorite among heirloom apple enthusiasts and collectors of English dessert apple varieties.

Pitmaston Pineapple is an English heirloom dating to 1785, named for a genuinely distinctive tropical, pineapple-like flavor and aroma that sets it apart from every other common apple variety, a quality that has kept it a beloved curiosity among heirloom apple collectors for well over two centuries. The small, golden-yellow, lightly russeted fruit is far smaller than a typical dessert apple, more the size of a large crabapple, but the intensity of its unusual flavor more than compensates for its modest size, making it a favorite for fresh eating in small quantities and an interesting addition to hard cider blends. The compact tree bears reliably; harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and expect a short storage life typical of many aromatic heirloom dessert apples.
